title: Lotus Sutra 2
speaker: Zoketsu Norman Fischer
summary: Zoketsu Norman Fischer suggests that the Lotus Sutra's teachings on bodhisattvas receiving prophecies of Buddhahood can be seen as a "skillful means" - a clever trick or expedient action used to help others escape suffering and find true liberation. This teaching challenges our conventional understanding of truth and reality, much like the intricate social structures of nature, such as that of the weaver ants. By using this approach, the Buddha is able to tailor his teachings to each individual's unique circumstances and growth habits, ultimately revealing a universal Dharma that transcends limitations and conceptual frameworks.

sentences.text: *The African and Asian weaver ants date back 50 million years to the late Eocene epoch.
And they live in the tree crowns of tropical forests.
These ants dominate much of the canopy and not only because of their large size as individuals, but also because of their large populations.
Mature colonies contain more than 200,000 workers.
A remarkable system of communication allows the colony to occupy the tops of several trees in areas spanning tens of thousands of square feet.
And like the Roman Empire at its peak, this territory is connected tightly by networks of trails.
The ants also maintain garrisons from which workers go out to collect prey and defend the nest.
They make part of their domiciles, which include tunnels and pavilions, from silk.*
*They also use silk to bind leaves and twigs together.
There is only one mother queen in each colony.
She is attended by her daughters.
The colony is an all-female society.
Males are reared and kept in the nests for short periods and are present only to inseminate a virgin queen on nuptial flights.
They die immediately after performing this duty.
The workers of this species are divided into two castes according to size.
The major workers take care of most of the quotidian tasks of the colony, including nurturing the queen, hunting and building and defending the nest.
The minor workers specialize for the most part in caring for the young.
They are the nursing caste.*
*Each colony has hundreds of pavilions, clusters of leaves held together with webs of silk.
The pavilions near the periphery of the colony's territory are occupied primarily by the oldest workers, the ant group that generally comprises the warriors in ant societies.
These are the ants most prone to risk their lives in defense of the colony.
Thus, one basic difference between human and ant societies is that whereas human beings send their young men to war, ants send their old women.
Another difference is that whereas we orient ourselves and communicate chiefly through sight and sound, ants do so largely through taste and smell.*

*In most species, the body of each worker contains between 10 and 20 exocrene glands that release chemical secretions to the outside of the body in one manner or another to be smelled or tasted by fellow members of the colony.
These secretions variously alarm, recruit, identify members of the colony, identify caste, and so on.
The weaver ants have what may be the most complex chemical system known in the animal kingdom.

The workers have no fewer than five separate recruitment systems, which are distinguished by the context in which the pheromones are delivered as well as by tactile signals the ants present with them.*
*For example, how they tap, approach, rush at, or stand above other ants.
The combined signals inform the ants of the situation and cause them to respond accordingly.

Translated into English, the five recruitment systems of the weaver ant are enemy close by, enemy at long distance, new territory discovered that we can reach, new suitable site on which to build pavilion and food.
Perhaps even more remarkable is the way in which weaver ants build a pavilion and on which their common name is based.
Their labor is highly specialized and coordinated.*
*First, mass formations of workers apply the pressure required to fold leaves and bring them together so that they can be bound by silk.
The ants form a living chain by grasping each other about the waist.
The one at the end grabs a leaf to pull it and curl it over.
If a single chain does not suffice, the ants form themselves into sheets of living chains to make the vegetation conform to their needs.
When the leaves are properly lined up, specialized workers bring out their immature sisters, small grub-like larvae that are at a late stage in their development and employ them as living shuttles.
A worker puts a larva's head down on the spot where it wants a silk thread to be released and touches the larva with its antennae, giving it a precise signal to release a strand.
As the larva lets out a strand, the ant pulls it sideways to the edge of another leaf.
This process is repeated literally thousands of times until the larva has no silk left with which to spin a cocoon.
But it doesn't matter.
The naked pupae are protected in the fearsome colonies and come to maturity anyway.*
So I read that to illustrate the point that such a thing is no more or less likely than the universe of the Lotus Sutra.
We were complaining last week about how preposterous and imaginative and unlikely such a thing was, that there would be Buddhas flying through the sky and realms and so forth.
But really, truly, that is no more or less likely than such a thing.
Who notices?
We don't know anything about this.
We're just taking Edward O.
Wilson's word for it because he's a reputable scientist.
I've never seen such a thing and you've never seen such a thing.

If we go down into the world of bacteria and viruses and subatomic particles, we'll see just as much preposterousness in the so-called external world as we can find in the internal and imaginative world.

So the point of the extravagance of the Lotus Sutra is to propose to us an inner imaginative world which is not based on space-time conceptual aspects of the outer world and the inner world that we usually operate on.
In other words, the world that we live in is rather a small construct based on our capacity as human beings to perceive space and time and concepts that make sense to us.
This world in which the chief concept is me and you.
It's one of the most important concepts that we have, me and you.
I am over here standing over against this world with all these other scary people in it, all these other scary big pieces of stuff, trees and rocks and so forth.
That conceptualization is the reason why we suffer.
The Lotus Sutra is proposing a world in which those conceptions are not the operative conceptions.
That's why it goes into such immense detail about time, for instance, lengthy periods of time and space.
Did you notice that half of the fantastic stuff about the Lotus Sutra has to do with time and space?
Vast amounts of time, vast impossible amounts of space.
What that's telling us is that our concepts of time and space are limited concepts.
Time and space are not limited to our concepts of time and space, which is something that Kant also figured out and so did the nuclear physicists after Einstein.
We live in a narrow world of suffering bounded by ego and physical restraints.
Number one.

Number two: a linear view of practice is that we can understand how that world of linear constraints and ego works, recognizing the Four Truths, recognizing that because of desire and clinging, we have created such a world.
So we can make a lot of effort over a long period of time to undo that misconception, and then we can finally achieve the path.
After much effort and much work in a linear way, we can become released: early Buddhism.
Still, in some way, you can see it operating in the same framework, but trying to use that same framework to correct the suffering.
Or we can recognize that that linear framework was never the way it really was anyway.
From the very beginning, it wasn't so.
From the very beginning, our limited sense of what the world is and what we are was just that, a limited conceptual sense.
In fact the world is much bigger than we know, much more imaginative and vast and wonderful than we ever knew, and we ourselves have been Buddhas from the first.
The world of limitations has never been limited.
This is the point of view of the Lotus Sutra.
That's why it's looking at the older schools of Buddhism and saying, well, this is good as far as it goes, and it was a necessary teaching in its time.
But in fact, reality is much more vast and open and wonderful than that.
So, although I think the Zen school toned down quite a bit the extravagant poetry of the Lotus Sutra, it really does also share this vision.
And I think we also are trying to share a vision of our lives.

In other words, as Bodhisattvas opening up and changing the world, using the stuff of our lives, our challenges, our difficulties, our problems, not as challenges and difficulties and problems to find peace in, but rather tools for the way, things that can be transformed as food for thought for the way.
This whole world, as the Lotus Sutra teaches, can be viewed as skillful means.
The world of limitations is not the world of limitations.
It's what we are given as the skillful means for our path.
I'm just sort of going back to the basic point of what we're doing here and what the Lotus Sutra is teaching and why it really is sort of sensible and relevant.
And I say that as we're about to launch into more extravagance.
Last time we did the first couple of chapters, and we're going to do chapter three and four and five or something like that tonight.
So I practiced up for you all over the weekend.
I was in Bellingham and I did the whole Sutra in two days, at the retreat in Bellingham.
We did do it.
We went through the whole thing.
So I was warming up so that I could practice up for you.
No, we sat.
We sat quite a bit.
We had two sessions a day of a couple hours.
And what we did, and what I'd like to do the rest of our time this month, is I would go over a certain portion of the Sutra, then take a short breather, and then discussion.
So, in that way, I think in five sessions we can probably get through it.
Because there are some chapters I think are easily skipped.
There are some that are more important than others.
So the third chapter.
Remember, in the second chapter the point was made that the teaching of the Buddha is infinite, because beings are infinite.
Each one is different, so each one requires another teaching, and that's what skillful means is, the ability to know and understand each person and what each person needs.
And that's why, since beings are numberless, teachings are numberless, and that's why only a Buddha could understand the immensity of teachings.
And then it said there, that's why the path cannot be explained.
Remember, we talked about that in early Buddhism.
There was a good explanation.
You could follow it and make sense of it.
That cannot be explained, but it can be indicated in parables.
And the Lotus Sutra is famous for its parables, and now we find in this third chapter the first really famous parable of the Lotus Sutra.
It's going to take us a minute to get to it, and tell a little story before we get there, but it comes up in this third chapter: the famous parable of the burning house.
So this chapter begins with Shariputra dancing with joy to hear this new iteration of the teaching of the Lotus Sutra.

And he says, in the past, as an arhat, as a practitioner of the old way, when I heard this sort of thing preached by the Buddha and I heard about bodhisattvas receiving prophecies that they would attain Buddhahood sometime later, I felt left out.
I felt like this wasn't about me.
And now I find that if we had been willing to just wait until this teaching was preached, then we would have obtained release through the great vehicle.
But we failed to understand that the Buddha was employing skillful means and preaching what was appropriate to the circumstances.
In other words, the early teachings, we took them at face value and we didn't really wait long enough and realize something better was coming along.
So darn, I guess it's too late for us.
We're deprived of these benefits.

So then, and this is repeated in verse, the Buddha says to Shariputra, no Shariputra, don't you know that in the past, under 20,000 million Buddhas, for the sake of the unsurpassed way, I have constantly taught and converted you?
So you thought, your limited conception of reality makes you feel like you were doing something else and you missed out on this teaching, but actually in many past lives you already were doing this.
You already were doing that.
In the past I taught you to aspire and vow to achieve the Buddha way, but now you forgot that.
You forgot that you already were doing it.
And you're in despair now.
You think you already attained extinction, and now it's too late for you, but now I'm here to make you remember the way you originally vowed to follow for the sake of everyone.
I'm preaching this vehicle called the Lotus Sutra.

Furthermore, just the way for all these Bodhisattvas I predicted, remember one of the elements that's in the course of life of every Buddha is that the Buddha receives a prediction of Buddhahood from another Buddha.
This is a really important point, that the way to Buddhahood requires a relationship with another Buddha who predicts your awakening.
Shariputra now learns that he's receiving a prediction from the Buddha, just like all the Bodhisattvas.
It turns out that the Arhats, who were bemoaning the fact that they got left out, were never left out, because in past lives they're part of the club, and they also receive a prediction.
And Shariputra then gets his prediction.
He's going to be such-and-such a Buddha with such-and-such a name, and such-and-such a Buddha field, and so on, and so on, and so on.
Well, this is really great news, and everybody is now filled with joy and dancing without end.
Now, you can't imagine, in the old sutras, the monks hearing teachings and dancing without end.
In the Lotus Sutra, people are constantly dancing and singing and pelting each other with flowers and jewels.
Before that, everybody was wearing shredded clothes and material taken from shrouds and going around meditating on death and the unloveliness of the body.
This is totally the opposite.
This is like meditating on the gloriousness of reality.
So they're all dancing up and down, enjoying each other.
And this is the part that I like.
I like the little details every now and then.
Yeah, the Hasidic, right, Hasidic Buddhists.
It's very much like that.
It's sort of like the Hasidic Jews are to normative Jews as the Lotus Sutra Buddhists are to the old way, right?
But here they're dancing around, and they start taking off their clothes, it says here.
*Each one removed the upper robe that he or she was wearing and presented it as an offering to the Buddha.*
This is not only the regular people there, but also the gods were doing this, the kings and gods, and they had gorgeous heavenly robes that they were offering to the Buddha, which they scattered.
The Buddha received all these robes, like the great Tibetan teachers who received immense numbers of gifts.
They receive them, thank you very much, and they toss them somewhere.
So the Buddha received all these gorgeous robes and tossed them.
And then the heavenly robes that they had scattered rose up into the air and became suspended in the air, and they were floating in the air.

Picture this, this giant assembly of Buddhas, bodhisattvas, here these robes floating in the air, and they're turning round and round of themselves, spinning around in the air, these gorgeous brocade robes.
And while this is going on, the Buddha, I think it's the Buddha, says, in the past at Varanasi, the Buddha first turned the wheel of the law.
Now the Buddha turns the wheel of the law again, the wheel of the unsurpassed, the greatest law of all.

So in other words, this teaching of the Lotus Sutra, that is so different in tone and feeling and sort of vision of reality from earlier Buddhism, is a second turning of the law, almost like a second iteration of the teachings.

So Shariputra says, well, thank you for this teaching and explanation, and I really feel good about it, but could you please, would you now maybe give some teaching so that others like myself who might have been confused about what was really going on can understand better?
Can you give us some teaching about this?
And that's when the Buddha gives the famous parable of the burning house.
And here's the parable.
*Shariputra, suppose that in a certain town, in a certain country, there was a very rich man.
He was far along in years, and his wealth was beyond measure.*
This is on page 56, for those of you who are interested.
He had all kinds of lands and everything, but he had one big rambling house, and this is the important thing about this house: it had only one gate.
It only had one gate.
And he has lots of sons who live in the house with him.
The house is very decrepit, falling down.
It's kind of a ruined old house.
Why a wealthy man wouldn't get his house renovated it doesn't explain, but he didn't.
So he has a lot of sons, 10, 20, maybe 30 sons.
It's funny, compared to the Lotus Sutra, the Bible.
The Bible says so-and-so had this son, and this was his name, and he lived for so many years.
The Lotus Sutra says he had some sons, maybe 10, maybe 20, maybe 30.
We don't know how many sons.
It doesn't matter, but he had a bunch of sons.
Anyway, the house all of a sudden is on fire, and the fire is closing in on everybody, and the suffering and pain of this fire are about to do in the man and his sons.
The man is running out of the house, but the sons are not paying the slightest bit of attention to this danger, and they don't even think of trying to escape.
Why?
Because they're playing games.
They're distracted.
They have many distractions, being sons of wealthy fathers.
They must have a lot of toys in their room, computers, different games they're playing.
They're engrossed in all this.
They don't even notice the flames because of their distractions.
And the man thinks, boy, this is a terrible situation.
If I don't get my sons out of here all at once, we're all going to be burned.
Now I have to invent some skillful means so that it will be possible for the children to leave the house and escape harm.
Now, the father is, it says, I can't find exactly where it says this, but the father is a very capable and strong guy, and first he thinks, well, why don't I just carry them out, get them out?
I can't get them motivated, so I'll just carry them out.
I could wrap them up.
He thinks, I'll wrap them up in a big blanket, and I'll put them on this bench and tie them up in a blanket on the bench, and I'll carry the bench out.
I can do this.
He's very strong.
All 30 of them he can carry out.
The trouble is, there's only one gate to the house.

The way the house is built, you see, even though he can carry them out, they won't fit through the door on this bench, so even though he's capable, theoretically, of getting them out of the house, he has enough power to do that, he can't do it.
They've got to get out of the house on their own steam, because that's the way the house is built.
So now he has to figure out some way of getting them out.
So he tells them, and he knows the sons very well, he knows what kinds of playthings and toys and distractions each one likes.
So he tells each one about something outside the house that they should come and get.

He gave each of them a carriage, and he says to the one who likes goat carts, there's a goat cart outside for you, to the one who likes deer carts, there's a deer cart outside for you, to the one who likes ox carts, there's an ox cart outside for you.
There's only one cart outside, drawn by a white ox, but he knows if he tells them that, they won't want to go outside.

So he tricks them by telling them that there are all these different carts outside, and they get excited about the carts because they're more fun than the things they're playing with, and they run outside the house, and when they get outside the house, he says, well, there's just this one cart, and they're saved and happy because they get out of the burning house.
So that's the parallel.
Now, I have a very, very strong personal relationship to this parallel, because I'll never forget when I was young, the first time I read the Lotus Sutra.
I was in my early 20s, and I read the old, I think it was the Soothill translation, the oldest one, and it's full of flowery, wonderful language.
I happened to be, at the time, staying with my parents.
I was living, I think, in California, but I went on a visit home, and I took the Lotus Sutra with me.
When I would go home to visit my family, I would always do a lot of practice.
There was nothing else to do, so study and practice.
So I was reading the Lotus Sutra, and I read this parable of the burning house for the first time.
I had never heard of it before.
And all of a sudden, I had this very definite feeling that was like a certainty.
There I was in my parents' house, and I thought, this house is burning now.
In other words, with suffering.
Now, it wasn't that, no, my parents were fairly ordinary and normal people.
They didn't have major problems other than just being human beings in the world.

But it was the first time I realized that the normal life that I had grown up in was actually a life of enormous suffering, even though, like I say, many people have in their lives obvious and spectacular suffering.
I didn't really have that.
Nevertheless, I got it, that this was a burning house, and that I was in this house with my parents, and we were in this dire situation.
And just like these sons, I couldn't explain it.

If I had said to my parents, we're in a burning house here, this is a dire situation, we've got to do something, they would have looked at me as if I was insane, the same way that the sons would have responded if this man had approached them and told them this.
They would have said, what are you talking about?
We're playing with our games.
We're busy.
Don't talk to us.
So I understood the meaning of this very viscerally and very personally.
It was actually quite shocking to me.
I'll never forget the feeling of those days, thinking about that.
Anyway, that's the parable, and then the Buddha explains, as if we didn't already understand the meaning of this parable, he explains in detail.

First, he says, when this rich man impartially handed out to his sons these big carriages adorned with rare jewels, having told them that it was a goat cart and a deer cart and it's not, was he lying to them or not?
Was this a lie?
Because that's the first thing that occurs to most people: gee, this is Buddhism.
You lie to people and deceive them to get them to do what you...
Yeah, right.
The end justifies the means.
So the answer here, in my opinion, doesn't really answer that objection, but I'll read you exactly what it says.
The Buddha puts this question to Shariputra: *Do you think that this man was deceiving his sons?* And Shariputra says:
*No, World Honored One.
This rich man simply made it possible*
This is on the bottom of page 58.
*for his sons to escape the peril of fire and preserve their lives.
He did not commit a falsehood.
Why do I say this?
Because if they were able to preserve their lives, then they had already obtained a plaything of sorts.
And how much more so when through an expedient means they are rescued from that burning house.
World Honored One, even if the rich man had not given them the tiniest carriage, he would still not be guilty of falsehood.
Why?
Because this rich man had earlier made up his mind that he would employ an expedient means to cause his sons to escape.
Using a device of this kind was no act of falsehood.*
So this may or may not answer our objections, but what he seems to be saying here is, from the standpoint of a limited truth and a limited reality, I suppose it is a falsehood.
But in the bigger picture of things, it really isn't a falsehood, because the sons are truly getting what they really want.
And if this is what it takes for that to happen, then this is what I need to do.
So it's a dangerous sort of thing, because we could always kid ourselves, well, I'm doing this for your own good, so I'm deceiving you in a thousand ways for your own good.

On the other hand, I think there's something to this, that sometimes in the Dharma, or a Buddha has to, as it says in some of the sutras, sometimes you have to break a precept in the name of compassion, in the name of something that's truly helpful.
And I always give the example of the person who is in 1945 in Germany harboring in their home Jews, and somebody knocks on the door, Gestapo, and says, are there any Jews in here?
And the person answers, utterly truthfully, no.
Because it's a deeper truth to protect these people than it is to be literal-minded about some words in an extremity like that.
And I think, so this is a dangerous kind of a thing, But nevertheless, that's what the Buddha seems to be saying here about skillful means in this case.
So there's a higher truth, a higher good that's being pointed to.
Anyway, that's what it says.
And the Buddha goes on to explain that, of course, the rich man is the father.
The father is the Buddha, because the Buddha is like this: the Buddha is the father of all the world.

The Buddha's job in the world is to see that the house is on fire and to save living beings from the fires of birth, old age, sickness and death, care, suffering, stupidity, misunderstanding, and the three poisons, to teach and convert them and enable them to attain perfect enlightenment.
That's the Buddha's job.
That's why the Buddha comes into the world.
So in that sense he's just like the father.
And yes, living beings are like the sons, all of them distracted and amusing themselves, unaware, unthinking of what their real situation is.
They feel no sense of danger when they should.
They make no effort to escape their situation.
And then the Buddha says, like that man, I too, as the Buddha, have the power to lift everybody up and carry them out of this situation, but I can't do that.
Because of karma.
The house is not built that way.

Even though I had the capacity, the house is not built that would enable me to take them out, because sentient beings, these living beings, have not yet escaped from birth, old age, sickness, death, care, and suffering, but are consumed by the flames in the burning house that is the three-fold world.
How could they be able to understand the Buddha's wisdom?
They must confront their own karma and walk out on their own steam, even though I may have to help them along by a kind of ruse to see what they need to do.
They need to do it.
And they're needing to do that because of the way the house is, the way karma works.
It doesn't contradict the immense power that the Buddha has, but despite the Buddha's immense power, we're all in the end responsible to make that effort ourselves.
And he explains that the goat-cart lovers were actually the Shravakas, the old school practitioners, the deer-cart people are the Pratyekabuddhas, and the ox-cart lovers were the Bodhisattvas.
So the fact that the ultimate cart is pulled by a white ox tells you that the Bodhisattvas are the closest, but it's not even exactly them.
The white ox is different.
So that's the parable of the burning house.
And the verse repeats the same thing, except it's quite graphic about the mess that the house is in.

It talks about all the many animals in there and stinking excrement piled up, overflowing, and foxes and wolves and jackals in there, gnawing at the filth, and packs of dogs, and not only that, but goblins and trolls.
It's unbelievable that, never mind the fire, they should have run out long before the fire even started.
It's a good thing the house burned down, because it was such a wreck.
This is all given in the verse form, but not in the prose form.
So the three-fold world, past, present, and future, is a world of suffering.
It's a burning house.
We can't get the motivation to get out of that house on our own.
So we need teachings that will inspire us to go in the direction, down the road, outside the house, and we probably need teachings that suit our particular style of being confused or distracted.
Those teachings might not be, in the end, ultimately real, but as long as they do the job of getting us activated in our practice, they work.
Eventually, when we get out of the house, we realize, oh, all these teachings and all these complications are really unnecessary, ultimately, but in the event, I guess we needed them.

Now, in the verse section, in the interest of full disclosure and fairness, I have to tell you that the end of the verse form talks about those who have the faith to hear the sutra and all the benefits they will receive, and those poor souls who slander the sutra, and the many penalties that they will have to pay, going to hell and so forth.

If, for example, they should be born as camels or be born as donkeys, they'll be camels and donkeys with very heavy burdens to carry or getting whipped a lot, or they might be born in the body of a serpent, different things like that.
And if they're human beings, they might be deaf, dumb, and blind, and in poverty and want and so forth and so on, with water blisters, diabetes, scabs, sores, ulcers, and maladies such as these.

So with all religious texts of ancient times, one has to interpret in a learned way, one hopes, in dialogue with other people who are knowledgeable and faithful, thinking through seriously, not just saying, well, this means whatever we want it to mean, but thoughtfully interpreting.
But every now and then you find things that you must reject.
So I think it's very unfortunate here that somebody reading this could think, oh, I just saw a blind person yesterday.
I saw a person who was wearing a [unclear: "cap or C and everything"] on the street.
And they deserve to be there because in the past they slandered the Lotus Sutra.
I mean, people probably thought such things.

That's one reason why, in Asia, there wasn't a whole lot of social services and the feeling of let's take care of people, because it was their karma to be poverty-stricken people, and they must have done something bad to the Lotus Sutra or something.
In the West, the point of view is different.
The Bible and so forth honors the poor and the destitute.
And so we feel an obligation to benefit them, not because they deserve to be the way they are, but because they're unfortunate, we should help them.
It's our obligation.
There's that view in Western thought.
I think the Buddhist view and the Western view are joining forces on such things.
Contemporary Buddhists don't take these things literally.
And certainly the Buddhists have joined the Catholics and the Jews in doing much social service and so on in Asia now.
But we have to be honest that the Lotus Sutra has this.
And there are other, even more objectionable things in the Sutra that I personally would reject.
Anyway, that's the parable of the burning house.
